lines.text: Here is the question this topic answers. A nightly job reads one terabyte of order events from a fast local drive, and the team wants to read it from object storage instead.
Before anyone runs anything, ask what the best case could be. Not the typical case, the least time physics allows, each way.
By the end you will compute both numbers, and you will know the smallest setting that would make them match.
Begin with a feel for the scale. A read from memory costs about a hundred nanoseconds. The first byte from object storage takes about a hundred milliseconds.
Say the ratio to yourself before you pick: milliseconds are a thousand times a microsecond, and a microsecond a thousand times a nanosecond.
How many memory reads fit in one object storage wait?

tolerated.line: How many memory reads fit in one object storage wait?

lines.text: About a million.
A hundred milliseconds divided by a hundred nanoseconds. Scale it up: if a memory read took one second, the storage wait would take eleven and a half days.
That is why every latency chart in this course is logarithmic. On an ordinary axis the memory read would be invisible. Equal steps here mean equal multiples.
Now zoom into the chip. Inside it, latency is counted in clock cycles, not in seconds.
Intel's manual gives the first level of cache a handful of cycles, the second a few more, the third dozens. Main memory is two hundred or more.
At two gigahertz a cycle is half a nanosecond, so the first cache costs two or three nanoseconds and main memory about a hundred.
The two ends of that scale differ by a factor of about forty. Keep that ratio in mind.
Below memory, the waits jump by orders of magnitude.
A random four kilobyte read from a fast server drive takes about eighty microseconds, according to the maker's own figures.
A hard disk must wait for the platter to turn. The average rotational wait alone is over four milliseconds, and measured with sixteen requests queued, each random read still costs at least six.
Object storage answers in a hundred to two hundred milliseconds for the first byte, with medians in the tens for small requests.
Every drop down the page costs you roughly a thousandfold in latency.
One more wrinkle inside a single machine. A server with several sockets gives each its own memory, and memory attached to another socket is slower to reach.
In the measurements Drepper published for older server chips, remote reads were about a fifth slower.
The operating system places a page on the socket of the processor that first touches it. So a thread that later moves to another socket can leave its data behind.
The remedy is to pin memory to each node, and measure.

tolerated.line: In the measurements Drepper published for older server chips, remote reads were about a fifth slower.

lines.text: Now a distinction that people blur. Latency is the wait before the first byte arrives. Bandwidth is the rate at which the bytes then flow.
The two rank the tiers differently. Memory alone ranges from about twelve gigabytes a second on one core to hundreds on a full socket.
Object storage is the slowest to answer, and yet one machine can pull up to a hundred gigabits a second from it, if you give it enough requests at once.
A hard disk is slow on both counts. So a tier can be a poor first answer and a good firehose.

lines.text: Put both into one formula. The time for a transfer is a wait plus the bytes over the bandwidth. Alpha is the wait, beta is the bandwidth.
Read a megabyte and look at where the time goes. On the fast drive about a third is waiting. On a hard disk, most of it. On object storage, nearly all of it.
That tells you a rule of thumb. A request smaller than alpha times beta is mostly waiting. On this drive that is about half a megabyte, and on the disk more than three times that.
So small requests are the thing to avoid, and the formula says exactly how small.

lines.text: A lab you can run on your own machine. Read every number in a one gibibyte array of numbers, once in order and once in a random order.
It is the same count and the same memory. Think about what changes between the two walks.
Compare the two walks.
How much longer is random?
About twenty times, here.

Memory moves in lines of sixty four bytes. In order, one line serves eight numbers, and the processor fetches the next lines before you ask. At random, each read uses one number from its line and waits.

The processor overlaps several waits, which is why it is twenty times and not a thousand. Make each address depend on the previous read and the overlap disappears. Saying it is the same because it is random access memory is the mistake this topic exists to cure.
Latency is not a fixed tax. One request at a time pays the wait every time. With several in flight, the waits overlap.
Look at the arithmetic.
One read on the fast drive takes eighty microseconds alone, which is twelve thousand five hundred reads a second.
The drive can do a million a second, so reaching that needs at least eighty requests in flight. The maker measured it with a hundred and twenty eight.
The lesson: concurrency is how you buy back latency.
Now the floor. A job cannot finish faster than its bytes take at full bandwidth, or its waits take with the chosen number in flight. The floor is the larger of the two.
Compare the two examples. A terabyte read in order from the fast drive: a hundred and sixty two seconds of bytes against five of waiting, so bandwidth sets the floor.
The orders table read page by page at random from a hard disk: twenty nine seconds of bytes against nearly six thousand of waiting. Now latency sets it.
A floor leaves out every other cost, so a real run takes longer. But it tells you which term to attack first.
Apply that to something routine, scanning the orders table. A full scan is sequential, so its floor is the bytes over the bandwidth.
That is under a second from memory on one core, about a second from one fast drive, and about half a minute from one hard disk.
Now the useful consequence. If your scan takes a minute on that fast drive, the drive is not the problem. Look for what is spending the other fifty nine seconds.
Back to the question we opened with. From the local drive, a terabyte is bandwidth bound: a hundred and sixty two seconds.
From object storage in sixteen mebibyte ranges, that is sixty five thousand requests. One at a time, the waits alone take almost two hours.
With many in flight the waits shrink in proportion, and with about forty one in flight the floor matches the drive.
But each request also streams its own bytes, so a real run needs more. Measure the per request rate before you promise anything.

lines.text: Test yourself with three cases. A query goes row by row through an index, making two million random page reads, one at a time, from one fast drive.
Each read waits its full eighty microseconds. Multiply.
What is the floor?
About a hundred and sixty seconds.
Two million times eighty microseconds. That is a hundred and thirty times the time to scan the whole table in order.
With eighty reads in flight, the waits fall to about two seconds, and then the bytes become the limit. The same count of reads, a floor sixty six times lower.
Second case. You copy the orders table from a local drive to another instance, over one connection, with the instances not packed in one cluster group.
Think of the path as a chain.
Slowest link sets the speed.
What is the floor?
About thirteen seconds.

A single flow between ordinary instances is limited to five gigabits a second, which is six hundred and twenty five megabytes a second. The table's eight gigabytes takes thirteen seconds however fast the drive is.
A placement group raises one flow's limit, and several connections raise the total. The drive was never the slow link.
Third case. The nightly job reads the terabyte from object storage with eight requests in flight, and it takes eighteen minutes.
A teammate says the store is throttling you.
Is anything broken?
Nothing is broken.
With eight in flight, the waits alone come to nearly fourteen minutes. Eighteen is only about one and a third times that, so the job is near its floor. The number in flight is the limit.

The job sends far fewer requests a second than a key prefix allows, and its bytes need only about a minute and a half of a hundred gigabit card. Raise the number in flight, or use fewer, larger ranges.
